newsitem.title: QATAR: GCC finance ministers discuss unified tariffs.
newsitem.headline: GCC finance ministers discuss unified tariffs.

text.p: Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) finance ministers began a two-day meeting in Doha on Saturday to discuss unified tariffs, an issue blocked by disagreement among member states almost since the alliance was formed in 1981.

"The gap is mainly on a few items which we are trying to classify before reaching a unanimous agreement to forge a common customs union," Sheikh Hamad bin Faisal al-Thani, Qatar's customs director, told Reuters.
"We are trying to classify more than 1,000 commodities into three main categories- exempted from tariffs, basic goods with a tariff, and other goods.
"Most commodities have been classified. But work on some 70 to 90 items whose value does not exceed three to five percent of the total has yet to be completed," he said.
Sheikh Hamad said classification may not be finished at the current meeting, but he hoped ministers would meet a target date set earlier by the six Gulf heads of states.

The GCC's Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Oman agreed at last year's Doha summit to complete the classification before the next summit in Kuwait, slated for next December.

Standard customs tariffs among the GCC states range from four to 12 percent, with special tariffs for some industries. A common rate of between six and eight percent has been discussed as the most likely, if and when the duties are unified.
The tariffs issue is a hurdle in the way of a free trade deal with the European Union which could open lucrative European markets to cheap petrochemicals and other goods from the Gulf.

GCC and EU foreign ministers agreed in April to set a deadline of no more than two years to complete a free trade accord between the two trading partners- an issue under discussion for more than 10 years.

Unification of regional tariffs is also a prerequsite to a GCC common market, stipulated by a 1983 economic agreement, which also calls for the link-up of stock markets, removal of customs barriers and aligning of national currencies of the six states by 1999.
